idiom_name: pure decision module + thin effect boundary (core/shell split)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put every rule in functions that take their inputs as arguments and return a value, with all non-determinism (time, randomness, ids, environment, already-fetched data) passed in as data; put everything that talks to the outside world in a thin layer that reads the inputs, calls the core, and applies the returned decision. Nothing about the shape is special - the discipline is that the core never calls the shell and never performs an effect, and that dependencies point inward: the shell knows the core, the core knows only values. Where the language cannot enforce that, enforce it by convention and mechanically: keep the core's imports/modules free of IO, review for clock/logging calls, and prove purity with tests that construct values directly instead of using mocks. The classic component structure (a Core and a Shell with ports declared in the core) is only worth building where the decisions must describe effects rather than compute them; otherwise pure functions plus an entry point replace it.
code_sketch:
core(values) -> decision          # pure: same inputs, same decision, no IO

shell():
    world = read()                # effects: db, network, clock, files
    d = core(world.snapshot)      # one call, no rule branching here
    apply(d)                      # effects: write, publish, respond, log
pitfalls: The core starts taking a handle it can query ('just one lookup'), and the split silently degenerates into a layered service whose tests need mocks again and the split bought nothing.
The shell absorbs rules as it grows; every conditional added there duplicates a decision that belongs in the core.
Applying the split to I/O-dominated code: extracting a decision function with one input and no branching adds indirection without any testability gain.
Exceptions thrown from the core instead of returned as values: exceptions cross the boundary as invisible control flow, making the core's error paths untestable without integration tests.
The shell grows into a god object: workflows, orchestration branches and 'just one more lookup' accumulate until the shell holds as many domain decisions as the original mixed code.

Non-deterministic data structures in the core: HashMap, HashSet and other unordered collections produce different iteration orders across runs, which defeats deterministic testing even when all inputs are stable; pass a seed or use ordered alternatives.

Accidental effects inside the core: logging, metrics or tracing calls made from a function that appears pure - the most common silent violation, invisible in code review and fatal to deterministic tests.

Effect system over-engineering: wrapping every function in an effect type before the architecture is proven adds ceremony with no gain; start with convention and promote to types only when the boundary is stable.
Mutating the caller's data from a 'pure' function (sorting the argument in place, appending to it) so the shell's state changes behind its back and aliasing bugs return through the front door.
Universal purity: refactoring single-input helpers into core/shell pairs, or wrapping every call in an effect type, until the code is a ceremony of adapters with no logic worth isolating.

Wrong move: apply the split to a trivial CRUD endpoint or an I/O-dominated pipeline -> the extra core/shell ceremony adds indirection without meaningful testability -> instead keep the path direct and isolate only decision logic with real branching.
